utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kay, are you ready to continue the cross-examination of Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I take the opportunity to inquire into the following matter. A motion has filed for admission of evidence under Rule 92 bis by the Defence which is at least unusual that a 92 bis motion is filed when the Prosecution still presents its case. Since I do understand that the 92 bis evidence is relevant for a witness who will appear next week we'd like it know when the Prosecution will respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. By tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By tomorrow. So that we have time to consider it over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On that matter, for our part, we won't be objecting, Your Honour, on behalf of the Cermak Defence. If that saves me having to do a written filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's now on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record the Markac Defence also joins with Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, you were with us quite sometime in September. At the beginning of your testimony, you made a solemn declaration that you would speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I would like to remind you that that solemn declaration still binds you when giving testimony now. Mr. Kay will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Kay, You may proceed. And, Mr. Liborius, could I ask you to focus your answers very much on the questions that are put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about a topic today which arises from your statement. If we could just see the original language used. That's Exhibit P801. It's your second statement of -- dated 2005. We're going to be looking at page 5, and it's the third full paragraph down; and it concerns the interviewing of the refugees in the UN barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could have page 5 of the English on the screen. That's the Croatian language one there. It's page 5 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you look on the screen, it will be magnified for you, I hope. The third full paragraph down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can have it a little bigger. Those at a distance ... there you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Liborius? It concerns your statement here about the interviewing of refugees in the UN barracks. You say Mr. Cermak was very much control -- in control of this issue on the ground. You don't doubt he was taking advice from Zagreb. And you conclude by saying you don't feel that: "Cermak was acting in good faith and that his only aim was to get as many Serbs from the UN compound as possible. To him, I felt it was a game." First of all, in relation to this matter, did you have direct dealings with Mr. Cermak on this issue, yourself?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of the handling of the refugees or the persons in the UN barracks was mainly dealt with by my humanitarian officer, Mrs. Chelsea Renton. I remember, however, that from time to time we would have conversations with colleagues, and it was also one of the issues dealt with in meetings, I believe, with the EU ambassadors. But I will have to check with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What we're going to do now is look at various documents, most of which are exhibits in the case, about 90 per cent of them, which give the dealings and involvement of Mr. Cermak with this matter from those who were dealing with him directly, all right? The first document I'd like us to look at which is where this matter comes from is Exhibit D28, looking at paragraph 3 in the English, which is also paragraph 3 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could put the English documents up first, please, because the witness is an English speaker, and it might be quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that the agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the UN UNCRO dealt with those who were suspects who had committed violations of international criminal law? Were you aware of that? You see paragraph 3 in this document states that people are able to leave the Republic of Croatia; there are guarantees for security, except those who committed violations of international criminal law. Were you aware that this issue here is the main spring for the matter concerning the interviewing of people suspected of war crimes who were within the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could you just answer whether you were aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection of the agreement between UNCRO and the Croatian government was to address all the issues that was pertaining to the persons in the UN compound. As part of that, as part of that, the issue of interviewing and subsequent following the issues of persons who had committed crimes, it was one of those issues dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question, and it will be much better if you answer the question, because we'll proceed much more quickly. Were you aware of this matter within the UN/Croatia agreement. It's yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The matter was in the agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it being a fact of the agreement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had read this agreement, had you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it in the form it has on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you read this agreement at the time.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us go now to a transcript of a video-clip Exhibit D509. This is a press conference given on the 8th of August by the minister of the interior, Ivan Jarnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During this press conference, he finished his statement by saying: "We have been monitoring the events and the crimes that have been committed in the occupied area, that we have a mass of evidence we handed over to the Tribunal in The Hague. Based on the facts that we have collected and we are now conducting interviews with those persons and those persons that could possibly be accused of committing certain crimes in that area." Were you aware that the Ministry of Interior, which had established the collection centres described in here, was dealing with the issue of the interviews of people in such centres?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not fully sure I understand the question. The interviews in the centres located at the coast-line or where?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. Let's just take the liberated area. The Ministry of Interior established collection centres by various orders; we know of that in this courtroom, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm asking whether you were aware of the fact that this was an issue that was headed up by the Ministry of Interior concerning interviews at the collection centres. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear to me that there were Ministry of Interior police personnel at these centres so that they were a part of it; yes, it was pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to Exhibit P388. This is a letter dated 8th of August, 1995, from General Cermak, sent to General Forand concerning the refugees in the camp, asking for a list, referring to the conditions of normal life, and in the last -- second-to-last paragraph: "It is necessary to make a list of men aged between 18 and 60 who will have to be interviewed by representatives of the civilian police of the Republic of Croatia in cooperation with your people. They will be provided with health care, access by the Red Cross and other humanitarian organisations. All those who have not committed crimes also be allowed back to Knin while those who do not want this, may be given transport to Bosnia or Serbia. Those detained will be handed to the judicial authorities of the Republic of Croatia." Were you aware that General Forand and General Cermak were dealing directly with each other upon this issue?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that it was General Cermak who said that interviews by the MUP could be in cooperation with your people, meaning the UN?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that the General Forand said that he had conversations with General Cermak about the procedure under which these interviews and the whole handling of the refugee group inside the UN compound would be carried out. I recall that it was the subject of quite a few conversations. So whether General Cermak said, It will be your people, or General Forand said it, I'm simply not in a position to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will go and look at the documents then and see how this unfolded because you have given your views on the matter in the statement. If we turn now to Exhibit D619, paragraph 3, which is on page 2. And in paragraph 3, in the third sentence we can see in this report from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan on the 9th of August the report that he gave concerning the issue to the UN as recorded by him, and we see there: "CIVPOL have conducted one patrol with a HV escort in Knin and have attended a meeting between a committee representing refugees, and General Cermak during which it was agreed that they will be allowed to attend interviews of refugees intended to screen out war criminals." So another report on what General Cermak was seeking to achieve in relation to the interviews of these people. Is there any comment you want to make on that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comment is the issue of the interviewing and the whole handling of the group of persons was one that went on for quite a protracted -- quite a protracted time. And it was an issue where General Forand felt particular responsibility because it was people who happened inside his camp for reasons that, no doubt, will be clear to the Court; and that it involved a lot of discussions and that, so to speak, the positions as I recall it today, the Croatian authorities, including General Cermak, from the start of these discussions were a little bit different from where they ended, once the agreement was reached how to handle these people. I also want to comment that my impression was the issue of how the interviews to identify persons who had committed crimes was going to be conducted was particularly sensitive and that the Croatian side, from the start, wanted to do that themselves on Croatian-controlled territory, and that later on it was established that it would be also monitored by CIVPOL; it would inside containers, and there will be various procedures guiding that so as to secure some sort of orderly conduct of that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we go to Exhibit P359 now, and page 3 of this document. Well, we'll do it much more quicker by going to page 4 and paragraph (C) 8. This is a document that is dated the 8th of August, 1995, it's an UNCRO sitrep released by General Forand; and, again, it is a report of General Cermak meeting the detained people in the camp and describing measures which the Croatian government was prepared to take to allow them to get on with their lives. Did you ever see that document yourself that was handed out by General Cermak concerning those people in. It's not a trick question. It's just --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to -- to look at a paper being brought up to me. I want to read it. Thank you. Yes, and what was your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the document that was issued by General Cermak concerning the measures the Croatian government was prepared to take to allow those refugees to get on with their lives? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go to Exhibit D300, this is that document dated the 9th of August, 1995, headed: Information. And you can see it there in the English that various rights and liberties were set out which General Cermak had written on this document on that matter. Did you see this?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember having seen and heard the General having this list of promises and provisions made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And did you -- were you there when he publicly stated them as much in terms to the DPs in the camp?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. If we go to Exhibit D62 --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I want to add that the paper you present me here was being widely discussed also in town and -- and it was the subject of a lot of conversations in those days, all these provisions and guarantees that would be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then I'm prepared later on how we monitored the implementation of them. But we can get back it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we go to Exhibit D620.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a Human Rights Action Team daily report of the 10th of August. If we go to the second page where we have the heading: Refugees, displaced persons. Paragraph 5, paragraph 5 blown up, thank you. This tells us about General Cermak having a meeting with, in fact, Mr. Al-Alfi and General Forand separately and separately with the committee of the displaced persons, as well as a deputy minister. And it concerns the issue of the agreement about the interviewing of detained persons of draft age at the Sector South headquarters, which UNCRO and international organisations will monitor as appropriate. And can you see General Cermak said the interviewing process will start tomorrow; and Colonel Cermak, written here, reiterated the Croatian authorities availability in transporting detained persons to check their houses and in order to freely decide whether they want to Croatia or remain. And it says in a few cases the practice had been implemented. But can you see that here, that there was General Cermak, in fact, at a very early stage wanting these interviews to take place as well as agreeing on his part that they could be monitored by UNCRO and international organisations, and they could take place in Sector South. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read -- I read the words "the results" -- the words on the screen, I think was a -- the conclusion of, as I referred to earlier, these conversations. So if you want to say that I will here, now decide whether Cermak had that initiative at the start of that conversation, I repeat, I'm not in a position to say yes or no because I was not at that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, but you've made your view in a statement. You can change that point of view if you want to now and say --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly don't intend to that. Because I rely on my monitoring observations and what I gathered from my humanitarian officers from my own experience in the field and from my conversations with locals. So what I'm referring to in my statement is my consolidated opinion. If I'm asked to comment on papers where I was not participating in meetings, I'm afraid that I will adopt the same approach as last time we discussed how I could comment on a lot of other papers. You can present a lot of papers where the result of a long meeting or negotiation process; but I'm still not in a position to say yes or no or who took that initiate. I think that you should ask General Forand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have. But you're not to ask me questions.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you're to answer my questions in the courtroom. And what I'm asking you is: Were you aware from your monitoring that General Cermak at the start, his position was fully in line with the UNCRO and UN demands. Were you aware of that before you gave your opinion in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am aware of and what was in my statement was a result of my conversations with General Forand and the UN staff at that time and my other staff that followed that issue closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's go to another document there, as the Bench can see it. Let's go to Exhibit D310. This, again, is from General Forand, a sitrep of the 14th of August; and it's his commander's assessment we see on page 2. Commander's assessment, you'll see in the second sentence: "Despite negotiations with General Cermak and the apparent establishment of procedures to enable progress to be made, no real progress has been achieved to date, nor does it appear that any will be soon. Indeed, this is an suggestion that General Cermak will shortly not have any say in this matter. It is it ambiguous at this time as to who would assume real responsibility and decision-making powers." And down in paragraph 2, we can see the urgency of the matter: "Pressure must be brought to bear at UNCRO and UNPF levels to relocate refugee who is are in the Sector South compound." So what had happened, Mr. Liborius, was this, that General Cermak had proceeded with negotiations and said that there would be various safeguards but obstacles were being put in his way. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection was that the -- on one side, the declaration of measures and rights, as you referred to in the 9 August statement, and the realities seen on the ground reflected two different worlds; and I think that that is illustrated in the first paragraph of General Forand's statement. Whether that included -- or whether that means that the pressure in Zagreb should be increased there could be good reasons for that. I think the pressure throughout the chain of command down to the very last individual military police officer in the field was to be increased because what was the situation was that there was a lot of nice words issued; and, on the other hand, you saw those words not being implemented in practice throughout the whole chain of command from the top to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, on the face of it you will agree that we have looked at General Forand and General Cermak quite clearly coming to agreement; and General Cermak giving rights that the UN found acceptable. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can agree a lot on the face of it. That is the whole problem. When you look on the face of it, the problem is those who had power didn't follow the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It could also --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where that could be, from top to bottom, it's not for me it decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would you accept this issue, that this could also demonstrate that, in fact, General Cermak had no power.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we're back to the issue of how far does his power extend. I felt; and I discovered in my monitoring activities and so did my teams that his name gave increased access throughout the month of August, that his frequent reference in papers, Croatian newspapers, media, his meetings with all sorts of officials we have just looked at some UN officials meant that his authorities was broadening. I saw his authority broadening throughout the sector. And on the other side, you say on the face of it, it appears that he has no power and I think last time we met you, you portrayed him as basically being in charge of municipal garbage collection. Then I asked myself the question why on earth didn't he tell us so? And told that to all other persons he met. He kept meeting people, and I saw that his authority was broadening in the sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, it seems that Mr. Liborius doesn't share the suggested conclusions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Perhaps we can look at Exhibit D301.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is a document, you'll be aware of the fact that Mr. Cermak had met the detained persons in the camp. He'd had meetings with them. He'd had much discussion with them about staying in Croatia, guarantees of rights, and this was a document sent to him, headed: The refugees from Sector -- South Sector camp in Knin express their thanks to Mr. Cermak, 15th August, 1995, and signed by a man called Branko Pupovac and saying for helping them in these hard times as refugees, "And we want you to know how much we appreciate your help and concern you showed us." So that was certainly an expression there of what was happening there on the ground, don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That touches on one of the issues during my present occupation actually. If you look at the card on the right-hand side. It is one of these standard issues. You will in my trade always introduce a letter saying we very much respect and thank you and so on and will end with a lot of niceties. When you say certainly, I don't share that "certainly. We also had an issue last time we met that was a letter of Claudio Dei where you have on the one hand you have all the diplomatic niceties, and on the other hand you don't see the underlying concerns because that is not -- it's is not common simply to express that. And I see that it's one of these standard cards you would issue to almost everybody who had been concerned or introduced to the matter as a forward-looking measure of trying to improve your situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go to Exhibit P40.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I'm doing, Mr. Liborius, is taking us on a journey through all the UN documents that ended up with the interviews an ended up with the eventually lease of the people in set in a step by step basis from all the records. So Exhibit P40 if we turn to page 2, in the numerical form. It's page 3, in actual numbers, and go to paragraph 5. This document is from the 17th of August, events dated 18th of August, by Mr. Al-Alfi -- no, next page, please, and paragraph 5 under the heading: Refugees and displaced persons. And at this stage of the 17th of August, we can see from the Human Rights Action Team in Knin there was a tentative meeting scheduled with General Cermak the next day to discuss final arrangement for the departure of the great majority of DPs from UN HQ Knin, to Yugoslavia and Bosnia. It is becomes politically charged from the DPs and Croatian's viewpoint, urgently required solution; and it's also urgent is that DPs and other UN compounds in the sector three UN companies reported Croatian policemen showing up, demanding war criminals be handed over. So the headquarters in Knin was preparing a written request to General Cermak for a Croatian escort to bring those people promptly to Knin from outlying camps. Were you aware of that problem, that some displaced persons had gone to other UN bases outside Sector South where they'd taken refuge and that was causing a problem; and the UN wanted to bring those people to Knin so that they were in the Sector South camp? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was reading on the screen, did that reflect what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I was aware that there was a group of people, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you know the UN were asking General Cermak's request for help in that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you said that these people were outside Sector South. Reading the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I didn't mean that, Your Honour. I didn't mean outside Sector South camp, I think that's what I said, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard you say a different thing, and it is reflected on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the document reads "in the sector." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's not part of the issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want to know whether I miss something. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go now to Exhibit D56, which is the follow-up from that last document we were looking at. This is a document from Mr. Al-Alfi dated the 18th of August, and we need to go to page three of this document, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you see there that at a meeting with General Cermak, Mr. Al-Alfi, with others, handed over a formal letter asking General Cermak to facilitate moving all the displaced persons, numbering 55, accommodated inside UNCRO battalion locations, to move them to Sector South headquarters; and General Cermak gave his approval and -- for such movement to take place that afternoon under escort. Further down in the page, in the third paragraph, the Sector South issue is discussed, with General Cermak asking for a list of those who made a final decision to leave Croatia. The list was to be submitted in that evening by the UN, and there was consultation that he was informed about the ongoing efforts at UNPF headquarters level, in consultation with the government of Croatia to reach an agreement regarding the transportation of those displaced persons who opt to leave Croatia: "We also understood from General Cermak that the idea of carrying out investigations with the displaced persons may be limited to a very small number of the displaced persons, probably between 10 and 20 and that that they would ask for the handing over of those persons. It was said by Mr. Al-Alfi that the investigation should be carried out inside Sector South headquarters and then the individual cases shall be discussed between the UN headquarters and government of Croatia." Again, were you aware of that, that in fact, at this meeting here, General Cermak was putting forward very small numbers of people that would be needed for interview? Were you ever informed of that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that the number of persons wanted for close interviewing decreased throughout the days and the weeks, and I think that the paper we have in front of us here, you say from the 18th of August is an indication that, as I illustrated before, the two quite different positions coming to a merging point; and I understand from Mr. Al-Alfi's position and the words he spoke at that time that the insistence that it be carried out under orderly fashion inside the Sector South headquarters was contributing to the fact that the number decreased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us look now at the next stage in what happened, and bearing in mind what you have said there, let us go now to Exhibit P369. This is a sitrep from headquarters, Sector South. The part that we need to look at is page 3 and paragraph 8, under the heading: Humanitarian aid: "After a meeting between General Cermak and Senior Liaison Officer Sector South, it was agreed all refugees in unit locations should be relocated to Knin. General Cermak showed a great deal of flexibility and cooperation in compromising to finally resolve this long-standing and difficult issue. Once agreement was reached, rapid action followed." If we go to the last sentence: "All refugees also be offered the option of moving to Knin under UN protection or returning to their homes. This operation is ongoing at this time." Well, were you aware of General Cermak being described as showing great flexibility and cooperation in compromising this long-standing and difficult issue?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that the issue was -- was dealt with finally in a prudent fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go to Exhibit D311.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a letter dated the 19th of August, 1995 from General Forand to General Cermak, and it's a letter of appreciation - assistance in moving displaced persons. Were you aware that General Forand had sent a letter of appreciation in these terms to General Cermak for his help, cooperation, and what he did?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did verbally share the information with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us go to 65 ter 4123. This is one of the few documents not previously exhibited before, Your Honour. It's a document dated the 20th of August from Mr. Al-Alfi and confirms, if we can to page 2, top of the page: "General Cermak is expected to discuss details of the departure of the displaced persons as early as tomorrow. He is also expected to submit a list of names whom he would ask to be handed over to Croatian authority for war crimes. "On the 18th of August, 51 more displaced persons were brought from the various locations of battalions to Sector South headquarters. Once the procedure for the departure of the displaced persons out of Croatia is agreed upon, we should expect some more people from the villages to ask for the same." What we have looked at there is the successful completion of one issue, the displaced persons moving to UN headquarters at Sector South in Knin, and also still the outstanding issue of the whole refugees and those suspected of war crimes who were in Sector South headquarters. That's where we've come to so far at this date, Mr. Liborius. And you will remember that until this time, General Cermak had been talking about small numbers of people being interviewed and under circumstances where the UN had a role to play. Would you agree? That's what we've looked at.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have looked at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can that document be admitted as an Exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D894.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D894 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit D621, I've included for historical purposes in this narrative that it is important that we see every stage. Exhibit D621 was a letter by Mr. Al-Alfi to General Cermak on the 21st of August, 1995, in which he provides a list of persons who wished to leave Sector South camp and leave Croatia and seeking his agreement and ensuring or suggesting that there will be additional names of people not on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the list of people - we're not to go through it in detail - but it's on the second page of this document of names from the camp?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that a list -- lists were being drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can now progress from this document as there's no point in looking at all the names, Your Honour; and there's no point in broadcasting it, and move to Exhibit D312. Exhibit D312, I would like us to take particular care and attention as to where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the top of the page you can see when it comes on the screen security an information service, Knin garrison, dated the 21st of August, 1995, and it's sent to General Cermak. Can you see that, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is enlarged, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I saw you were taking notes then when I was introducing the document, but I'll repeat it, security and information service send this document on the 21st of August to General Cermak; and it's a list of names, list of persons at UNCRO camp in Knin against whom criminal reports have been filed for crimes against the Republic of Croatia. And, in fact, this document was greater than the numbers that General Cermak had been speaking about, which you'll recollect we noted. This actually goes up to 72 names, if we go to the last -- go to page 4. See, 72 names. So the security services had sent Mr. Cermak this document, telling him that these people, 72 names, were those wanted, suspected of war crimes. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen the Croatian service letter to General Cermak before. I was, however, aware of the general discussion that was in the area at that time, that a number of Croatians felt that the UN garrison was one big safe haven for war criminals and that they wanted to lay their hand on them. I haven't seen that -- that for obvious reasons, that particular document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, pertinent to this issue that we've just looked at Mr. Cermak was talking about far fewer numbers of people, 10 or 20, and then there comes about a change caused by the security services. Were you aware that, in fact, it was others and not Mr. Cermak who sought increased numbers of people for questioning?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of 10 or 20, as we looked at before on the 18th of August, I think was the result of intense discussion, as I said previously, and the -- from a starting point where the numbers were quite higher. I don't know if that satisfies your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think we've seen that the starting point was numbers lower and this has now been increased by another agency.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the atmosphere on the, so to speak, on the Croatian side of the table from the very start of the issue was, as I said, the UN compound was a safe haven for criminals. We have to have them all. We will have to conduct our own interviews. We will decide ourself how and where; and then through intense discussions and mainly through insistence on the side of General Forand and his staff that a compromise was reached where both the procedure was different to that of the Croatian intention from the start and the number was lowered. Now, the inner deliberations between the Croatian authorities, the documents you present me here, I would just expect as natural. I haven't seen the paper before but it comes as no surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us now lock at another document in this chain because we're in fact looking at these negotiations, Mr. Liborius, as to what was said and done at the time. That is exhibit 65 ter 1220. And it is a Sector South sitrep report of the 26th of -- of the 21st of August from General Forand. And you can see in paragraph 3 on the first page: "Meeting with Croatian authorities. The military governor of Knin asked to meet commander Sector South, at HQ Sector South. Discuss issues including displaced persons." We see the main topic of discussion was the departure of the displaced persons under UN protection at headquarters Sector South and the question of when the Croatian authorities would be willing to allow them to leave. Mr. Cermak had been provided with a list of the 687 persons, we've seen that, out of a total population of 731 who wished to leave, including people at the hospital. And, at this point, Mr. Cermak indicated he now had a list of 74 persons under suspicion of war crimes: "He said he thought the list was too long and could be shortened. He also said that once he provided the list of persons for who there was proof of war crimes, then these persons must be handed over to the Croatian authorities." Well, from that statement there, doesn't that contradict your statement that you gave in Exhibit P801: "I did not feel Cermak was acting in good faith, and his only aim was to get as many Serbs from the UN compound as possible." Doesn't this contradict what you have asserted there, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily, because, you see, I just happen to have a glimpse at the last page there with the list of the names; and I saw one of the ladies named Renata somebody with a remark saying, Maybe she was the sister of some minister. And you arrive at a different conclusion because I think you failed to realize or illustrate the first discussions that went on in which, as it was told to me by UN staff who conducted that, it was quite tough talks about how you handle this issue and you cannot just -- where their position was you cannot just throw a number saying everybody who would be in the camp would be liable for blanco [sic], claims that they were war criminals, and we have to interview them. And during such negotiations I would call them gloves-off talks. There comes a point where it was brought to General Cermak that have you to present some sustainable information what you want these persons for, what you allege that they have done, and in that process you grind down the numbers. Of course 20, 21st August the General would be perfectly aware that coming forward with a list saying again one of the names, just as an example, if you bring that previous display up, having that particular lady, Renata, why would you want to interview her because you suspect her to be a war criminal; she may be the sister of a minister. We have a process under which or during which the General is perfectly aware that such a thing would never fly that the issue having attracted international attention was a burning hot potato and that some resort would have to be achieved and you have to sacrifice your initial, quite overambitious approach. Whether that was the good, well, and honest intention of General Cermak from the very start, my monitoring activities did not suggest that and I think that one of the issues procedural issues that may, as I said -- we failed to see the complete picture, that when you have for example the letter from General Cermak thanking General Forand -- from General Forand to General Cermak thanking him for the assistance in bringing refugees from the UN camps outside Sector South headquarters, it is one of those typical letters you send to your opposite number when you want to hammer done your conclusion, I realize that you have accepted my point I want to thank you for being so cooperative; it is a standard diplomatic procedure and you fail to portray the full picture, that this is a true indicator that you have a very, very forward-leaning and constructive approach from the start of the negotiations. Had we had that forward dealing approach, I'm sure that we would have resolved that question very, very sooner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Haven't you contradicted yourself in relation to the evidence we were looking at because General Cermak started at 10. He didn't start high and work down. This is the point, Mr. Liborius, that you are failing to see, and don't you accept that, that by your very own statement you contradicted yourself. He started at 10 but then it was taken out of his hands and made greater. If you don't accept it, very well, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the -- the Al-Alfi paper from the 18th of August ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might this document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D895.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D895 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'll look at Exhibit D622 now, please, which is from Mr. Al-Alfi. It's dated the 21st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And for a complete picture, we've included this although it's his report of the same meeting. And as he saw it Cermak informed the meeting, in paragraph 2, about the list of 74 names. He further informed us he is continuing his contact with Zagreb to shorten the list possibly, he puts here, to 15 names or so, a figure that was missed out of the last report of the meeting: "General Cermak ruled out the basic idea of carrying out the interviews with all those names between the ages of 18 and 60 or any possibility of accepting that the interviews be carried out inside Sector South HQ." So, again, what he had greed to originally was now being ruled. He had agreed that that could take place in Sector South HQ, but now that was being changed. Did you appreciate that, that Mr. Cermak, in fact, was being overruled on matters?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you indicate, timing is crucial to understand the picture, that as the matter had been burning up until 18, 19, 20, 21st August, General Cermak was fully realizing that you had to arrive at a conclusion as you indicate in your previous -- one of your displaced Al-Alfi paper from 18 August where he mentioned the figure 10 to 20. So you see, so to speak from a high point you see a decrease in numbers and then we are now at 18, 20, 21st August, and then suddenly comes up further instructions from headquarters. I do not doubt that the papers you presented from -- from the Croatian service is accurate, but it is just an illustration that you will have had a process in the Knin area where intense discussions with General Forand and his staff arriving at a sensible way to handle this issue. Then this becomes, of course, evident to other agencies and then they try to bring back the situation as it was before this compromise was reached. To reach a compromise, you have to work on your opposite number and of course that was the result of many, many days but to suggest that you're -- the General Cermak originally had such, so to speak, low ambition, I think is actually contradicted in the display you show. So I do not feel an urge to change my statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's then turn to page 2 of this document because you gave us your views on negotiations, and it seems that Mr. Cermak is giving away all his cards, then, according to your argument because he pointed out that UN CIVPOL should be involved in the negotiations to be carried out by CRO POL. That is what is he saying, so he not taking an extreme position and giving away bits. He's actually said they can be interviewed in the camp, as we know at the start, you can be there, international organisations can be there, CRO POL can be involved in the investigations and UN CIVPOL as well. Don't you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 20th, 21st August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, that was fright the beginning. That was right as we saw on the 10th of August. 9th of August. So he is taking a remarkably liberal position with his negotiations, isn't he, giving away all these things. He is not playing the hard-ball game that you were saying that you might have done. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is going a bit in circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the interpretation of all my monitoring activity and that of my fellow colleagues is reflected in the -- in the brief paragraph. If we want to go on this in circles we can do so but I'm not sure it serves a purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us go to Exhibit P45 now, Exhibit P45. And that is the HRAT report of the same meeting that we've just been looking at, Exhibit D622. If we turn to page 3 here. And again I do this out of completeness so that it is followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: General Cermak said: "The UN can organise the convoy for the DPs accommodated in UN Sector South headquarters who wish to depart to FRY and Bosnia. However, he requested UNCRO hand over to the Croatian authorities 75 draft-age males currently in the UN compound. General Cermak stated those men would have be interviewed outside UN premises. UN CIVPOL will be authorised to monitor the interviews and UNCRO representatives reiterated their position. The meeting was adjourned. General Cermak promised to provide a shorter list, 15 names, including the males that are suspected of war crimes and for this reason have to be under Croatian custody. This matter is becoming more and more urgent and requires solution at a higher level." We've just looked at that, said that we've seen everyone's report of the meeting, Mr. Liborius. If we now go to Exhibit D624, this is another UN Sector South HQ sitrep report. If we turn to page 2, and it is heads: UNCRO meetings. And the ECMM is referred to this as being in addition to Sector South escort. So can you see General Forand chaired a meeting to discuss the movement of the IDPs. You can see who it was attended by, all the senior people, including the Red Cross. It was agreed that UNHCR would order buses for 800 persons, that it would be a departure on the 26th of August, convoy command will be the Senior Liaison Officer for Sector South, various agencies who will be escorts, approached to be escorts. A major issue remained to be addressed at a high level is the UN oversight of review of charges expected to be levelled shortly by the government of Croatia against some of the men being protected at the camp. And an answer to the question was urgently required. If we go to the next document, which is Exhibit D313 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, we give the French translators an opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit D313, which is a letter dated 23rd of August, and comes from the officer who was the Senior Liaison Officer we've seen referred to in this matter, Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk, who wrote to the Croatian army liaison office in Knin and responding to a request for a meeting on that day: "I have passed to commander Sector South your request for a meeting to deliver on the instructions of General Cermak a list of those persons under UN protection." It goes into the detail we've looked at. If we can go to the last six lines: "The disposition of those accused of war crime will be agreed on a case-by-case basis between the UN and the government of Croatia. If General Cermak is unable to proceed in this way, as we have agreed then the commander of Sector South would like to be informed in writing of the position of the government of Croatia so that the necessary higher-level negotiations may begin to resolve this issue."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's Exhibit D313, we should be looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think we're looking at a different document here. I don't understand how it happened. But it should be page 3 of this document, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My question was, as I am, I believe, asked to refer to two documents on the screen, I started to read, actually that particular document, and my question is: Some of these documents are best seen in their entirety, so if I could have time to read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you feel any need to read portions of the document, but I don't think the Chamber will allow to you read the entirety of the hundreds and hundreds of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, it was just the Tymchuk report we had in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, that appeared to be not the right document. So, therefore, Mr. Liborius, forget about that document. As Mr. Kay indicated, the wrong document was on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a letter from Colonel Tymchuk on the 23rd of August. Again, it's just put in as part of the picture, Mr. Liborius, so that all the documents are laid out as to what happened and who said what, what their positions were so that it is fully indicated. And you can see there in paragraph 2: "The disposition of those accused of war crimes will be agreed on a case-by-case basis between the UN government and the government of Croatia. If General Cermak is unable to proceed in this way, the command of Sector South would like to be informed of writing of the position of the government of Croatia so that necessary higher-level negotiations may begin to be resolved."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move on from there to the next document, which is 2D03-0058.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is an document dated the 23rd of August from General Cermak to General Forand; and it's the list of people against whom criminal charges were filed, it says in the document, regarding crimes against the Republic of Croatia who were in the camp. If we just go to page 2, we can see it was sent by General Cermak, to General Forand. And this time it is 62 names. So that was the position at this date, on the 23rd of August. In relation to that matter, were you aware of the names being reduced during the period that the UN and Croatian government were negotiating?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Given these slight reductions in number, according to your position, General Cermak would have been undermining the negotiations of the Croatian government, because he was suggesting 10 to 20 or 15 people. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The -- and I am afraid that we have to say that we're going in circles. The issue of the convoy departure at that point in time we are now into the 20s of August was as it was illustrated in Colonel Tymchuk's letter from the 24th of August. That the first list as it said in the paper was deadlined by the Senior Liaison Officer accepted -- he did not accept that, and again gave the position that the convoy cannot leave before these persons are handed over. So if you look at the procedure, the departure of the convoy was, to the best of my observations at that time, being obstructed, until a solution satisfactory to the Croatian side was found regarding the issue of the detained. I do not question - and that's important for you to understand - I do not question there was a need to find people who, no doubt, had, if you wish to say, blood on their hands. The procedure under which that is done, and the evidence that is brought forward of course was the centre of discussion; and I do not want you to portray that this issue of the detainees in my eyes was a matter of just getting everyone on the buses, out of there, that everybody on the buses who would be quite bad people get away with it. The issue was to get an orderly procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit, and I note the time for the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D896, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D896 is admitted into evidence. If the usher could escort Mr. Liborius out of the courtroom. We will have a break, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When should I be ready?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately 25 minutes, so we resume at approximately 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, the last question was a relevant one, not about the break, but when will I be ready. Could you give us any further -- microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just got 14 documents to go through. I have decided rather than dealing with other topics with this witness, I'm just dealing with this matter. It's entirety -- from our point of view, we feel it is important that the Trial Chamber doesn't get bits of information, that we have to go through it in a process so that the whole story is before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't keep a record on your efforts on one document, but in time that would be mean approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 45 minutes. Then Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't anticipate more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties could endeavour to see whether in one session we -- of course the estimate is now 1 hour 45 minutes to see whether in one and a half hour if you, Mr. Kuzmanovic, could save ten minutes and Mr. Kay another five minutes, because testimony of this witness takes quite a bit of time. I'm not blaming anyone for that, but it is of some concern. Mr. Waespi, how much time you anticipate at this moment you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: At this point, ten to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten to 15 minutes. Which mens that we should try to finish with this witness before the end of this morning's session. We have a break, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we look at Exhibit D626, and it's just a brief letter, dated the 24th of August from General Cermak to General Forand, asking to meet him with Mr. Al-Alfi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, again, this is just put in for completeness, Mr. Liborius, as I'm sure you'd appreciate, which is part of the narrative. We have it there. On the 24th of August, a meeting was arranged. And we now move to D627, we can see another letter dated the 24th of August, 1995; Exhibit D627. And Mr. Al-Alfi sent to General Cermak an update on the displaced persons and with that, there was a list of further names as had been forecast might happen by Mr. Al-Alfi when he sent the original list. Do you remember that, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We won't look at the name there, but it's just part of the narrative, and then we can get back to the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit D151, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document, again from Mr. Al-Alfi. As the contents of the message show, this was a report on that meeting that was requested on the 24th of August, and we can see that General Forand was there. The matters that were discussed were these: "General Forand ... informed that the position of the government of Croatia is that it would be impossible to start any convoy for the departure of the displaced persons presently accommodated inside Sector South headquarters until 62 persons wanted for war crimes are handed to the Croatian authorities. General Cermak repeated clearly that this is the last order he received reflecting the official position of the government of Croatia." Just on that matter there, did you appreciate that in fact General Cermak had been acting on instructions on this matter from higher authorities in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure up until that time, I'm sure, would entail discussions with higher authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see in paragraph 2 that the list was handed over. It didn't include the types of charges against persons. Page 2 of the document, and General Cermak was told that this was contrary to what was agreed upon earlier, on the 21st of August. And he replied that such information can be obtained from the courts in Croatian -- Croatia: "He informed us that his efforts to reduce the numbers of those included in the list were not successful," and this was the response he received from the government of Croatia, and he said an official letter would be sent. And the note here is: "According, this matter cannot be resolved at our level. It needs to be taken up at the higher level with the government of Croatia. This view is also shared by General Cermak himself."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry for going so fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you see here, do you agree that this is an indication that you have actually wrongly blamed General Cermak here for the obstacles and problems that were caused in these negotiations? It wasn't his fault that the position the UN wanted was not agreed by the government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question right, saying that I wrongly blamed General Cermak, then I will reflect my impressions from the time in August; and my statement is the consolidated view of the whole process --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To do what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's not your impressions I want. I have pointed out to you facts from the UN contemporaneous documents at the time, and I'm asking you the question; and that's all I want answered, is whether you accept you have wrongly blamed General Cermak for the problems concerning the displaced persons in the UNCRO camp and the issue of the alleged war criminals. And you can just say whether you agree or disagree. I don't want your impressions because I am putting facts to you.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with your way of painting things, because I think that you fail to see them in the order that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will look at the next document, which is Exhibit P374. This is the report of General Forand concerning that meeting on the 24th of August, so we're looking at it for completeness. And if we go to page 3 of that document, paragraph 2, where we see General Forand's note on the same meeting: "The military governor emphasised that the position of his government is that the first 62 persons must be handed over ..." And pointing out, in paragraph 3, that General Forand and General Cermak had a gentlemen's agreement on the 21st of August and pointing out in 4, that this matter "cannot be resolved at the Sector South level. It must be pursued between higher level UN authorities and the government of Croatia." So that is General Forand's same assessment of that meeting, Mr. Liborius. Will you agree or disagree with my last question I put to you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have, at earlier occasions, expressed my opinions. But it is bit like good cop/bad cop situation. Have you a situation where as I have described before and issue is becoming a burning hot potato; and some sense has been finally reached at a local level, and then of course there is inside discussions on the Croatian side, I don't doubt that. The issue of how this is it being tackled. I think that if we followed the line of argumentation that you're putting forward that General Cermak would have indicated from the start, we would have solved that earlier; but I said that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will just now look at another document, Exhibit 65 ter 4604 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Kay, Mr. Liborius, your last answer, could I understand that to be that you disagree with Mr. Kay that on the basis of the information we have in front of us and which apparently led General Forand to the conclusion that the matter should be resolved at a higher level that you disagree with Mr. Kay that, on the basis of this material, to incorrectly blamed General Cermak for the obstacles and difficulties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really to have read your question, Your Honour. I think it contained various elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, I'm asking the question since you didn't answer the question put to you by Mr. Kay; that's my problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood Mr. Kay's question whether I -- in my statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not discuss at this moment whether or not you answered the question. I got the impression you didn't. But let's -- if you answer my question, then that would be good enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part one of my answer, yes, I realized that it was going to be discussed -- resolved at higher level. Part two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you read my question. Mr. Kay puts to you the report by General Forand in which he expresses, as his view, that the matter should be resolved at a higher level. That's information that is presented to you by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay could like to know from you whether, on the basis of this information, and the information he earlier has put to you, whether you do agree or disagree with his suggestion that you incorrectly blamed General Cermak for the obstacles and difficulties that were encountered in relation to this issue. Do you disagree or do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I disagree when I described Mr. Cermak's activities throughout the month of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I can give an exhibit number to the next document as it has been in already. Exhibit D628. Exhibit D628.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is where General Cermak, on the 24th of August, that same day, sent the letter to General Forand about the official position of the government of Croatia, the terms of which we know concerning the handing over of the people and until they are handed over, those at the camp cannot be moved and that that was the official standpoint. Did you see that letter at the time?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the letter. I know of its existence. It was referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We've no need to look at that any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit D314, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a cable from Mr. Akashi in Zagreb dated the 25th of August, 1995 to Mr. Annan, Secretary-General, concerning the displaced persons in Knin. And that Mr. Sarinic -- did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, Hrvoje Sarinic was the present Chief of Staff or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he been in consultation with the Croatian Ministry of Justice. The Croatian government would not allow interviews with persons suspected of war crimes on the UN premises, and because of that the displaced persons could not leave the camp until the 65 were handed over. In paragraph 2, Mr. Sarinic refers to visits of suspects being arranged with investigating judges. Full documents would be made available. Paragraph 3, position of the UN concerning the 6th of August agreement and referring to the oral agreement between Croatia, General Cermak, and the UN, General Forand being pertinent. So did you appreciate that the government of Croatia had overruled General Cermak or any position he had made with General Forand was in fact not going to be followed by them? Did you appreciate that, that it was at a high government level that General Cermak's agreements with General Forand had been decided not to be followed? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a little bit like when we play the good-guy/bad-guy game in our diplomatic service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I'm not going to speculations about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, you're not invited to give your comments. The question simply was whether you knew, whether you appreciated that Mr. Cermak was overruled by the government in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the face of the papers here, there would be a suggestion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We've no need to look at the rest of the document, but for the assistance of the Court, there was a legal opinion that was sought by the UN. Your Honours may recollect that. It's been looked at in court when General Forand gave evidence. That's further on in the document, and I won't repeat evidence. Can we go to Exhibit D629, please. This is a document dated the 27th of August from General Forand, sent to General Cermak, saying: "It now appears our higher headquarters have been unable to make much progress ... I believe it is important to remind you that I do not have nor I do wish to have a copy of the list you offered on 24th of August." That was the list of 64 people or 65 people, which General Cermak had: "Until such time as I am provided a list of the accused that specifies the charges against individuals and clearance for the departure of all those not accused ..." He says he feels no obligation to enforce heightened security measures in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that there developed an issue between the Croatian government and the UN over the differences between the legal systems as envisaged by the UN of the Croatian system and the Croatian government as to how their legal system worked? Did you appreciate that the word "charges" caused -- was causing a problem as well between the parties?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that there developed a bunch of issues, one of them being how these charges were interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that the Croatian justice system did not have the charges system which was envisaged by those working within the UN? Did you appreciate that at the time?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did in my conversations with various police officials and other legal actors discuss the Croatian legal system from time to time. This issue here was, of course, a burning one in the weeks in August. I recall that there was differences in how these charges were -- were being interpreted, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit D632, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 30th of August, 1995. It's by the security information service, can you see that, on the top left corner? Sent to General Cermak. We saw the earlier document sent by them, list of people against whom criminal reports were filed because of criminal acts against the Republic of Croatia and who are in the UNCRO camp in Knin. Did you appreciate, again, that General Cermak was receiving details about these people from the security service?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have no need to look at the whole document, Your Honour, but it contains those details in similar form on the first page against the remaining 60, 62 people in all. Can we move to Exhibit D633, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This exhibit is dated the 31st of August, 1995, a letter from Mr. Al-Alfi to General Cermak, in which he sent to him lists of the various categories of people under protection. This is included just for the full narrative on the matter and to show what was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We don't seem to have it on the screen in English. Oh, it's gone high up the page. No problem. We can move on from that document because it is just the list of names, and the Court can appreciate the terms of the document. Can we move now to Exhibit D636.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a report from Mr. Akashi again to Secretary-General Kofi Annan on the 8th of September, 1995; and it concerns the negotiations with the Croatian authorities over the displaced persons and that they were at an impasse. It explains what was taking place at his meetings. And on page 2, if we go to paragraph 3, we come to the reason for what was described as the impasse on the first page, and Mr. Akashi reports: "The crux of the dispute at this point is the Croatian authorities' insistence ... about documentation to support the surrender ... of the men. There's a warrant signed by a judge requiring the person to appear before the investigating judge, and the UN wanted to review the details of charges and supporting evidence in each case." Did you appreciate that this matter came to become part of the blockage between the two groups in September, approximately a month after the problems started?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the letter ends, referring in paragraph 7 on the next page to a meeting with Mr. Sarinic and wanting Mr. Annan's views on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next series of documents, Your Honour, are documents from the office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for the former Yugoslavia, as headed, from the UN to Mrs. Skare Osbolt and if we look at Exhibit D637, Your Honour, these are documents that are outside the Mr. Cermak's involvement which I'm suggesting to the Court they can be dealt with as a collective on the issue, if that meets with the Court' favour without going into the detail?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi would you object to such --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the document I'm referring to are Exhibit D637, Exhibit D638, Exhibit D639, and Exhibit D640; if we turn to page 2 of 637, we see the date of the letter sent to Mrs. Skare Osbolt by Mr. Harston of the UN concerning the issue of the charge seats and the legal issues that the UN was now raising concerning the interviewing of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate, Mr. Liborius, that at a very late stage, not at the beginning of this matter, that legal officers within the UN were raising legal issues and international legal provisions concerning the interviewing of the suspected war criminals?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that, as the issue became more and more complicated, that legal issues, legal details, became, so to speak, the position from which the -- the trench war was being waged. So, yes, I do remember the legal discussions although I did not follow it in this particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know any reason why all these legal matters were raised at a late stage by the United Nations and weren't raised at the first opportunity down there on the 8th of August in Knin?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That actually brings us to the interpretation of how the whole issue of the people inside the UN Sector South headquarters was handled. My recollection is that the legal issues, how to conduct the interviews, how charges was to be interpreted, what is the charge, how should it be running, according to which set-up legislation and so on, was used as an instrument to get back and get, you know, as much out of the deal that you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, may I interrupt you there. The question was about timing. Why at a late stage rather than at an early stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it was a failure to resolve the issue from the first time. Had there been a will to get the issue solved then we could have solved it quite fast. Because that failure to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you again. Mr. Kay says all these legal issues came up at a rather late stage. Do you have any explanation why it wasn't done at the early stages whereas, as you explained the matter, it is that whatever could you find to obstruct you would use it, that -- now, Mr. Kay is asking why this, what you might consider to be an obstructive attitude or approach why it was only taken at the late stage and not the early stages by Mr. Cermak. Mr. Kay if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way I interpreted the situation was that, as the issue developed during the weeks of August, it attracted international attention. We saw -- asked to be referred to the Security Council. The legal issue was introduced lately -- later in the process, because it has an air of -- it does take -- it is appreciated that it takes more time, and you can develop your discussion from, so to speak, to the moral high ground; and therefore, you have good explanations as to why you cannot get the issue solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes that seems to be not an answer why it was invoked at a late stage. We've heard your explanation. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm endeavouring to finish on time. I will move very rapidly now because we're coming to the finish of the matter. Can we have Exhibit P387.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the documents that I referred to, Mr. Liborius, at Exhibit 640 the number of people suspected of crimes was reduced to 34, and we can see that part of the story taken up in Exhibit P387. Colonel Leslie and Colonel Blahna met with General Cermak and confirmed an agreement reached on the 13th of September for the departure of the people, the arrangements to be made, the time. Colonel Leslie was briefing the people in the compound, and the Croatian deputy minister of justice would be delivering the charges at 1300; and in the succeeded papers we have the various lists of names which we don't need to go into in any further detail. But what had happened by this stage was that it was 34 individuals had now been agreed between the parties, if the documents were supplied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we move to Exhibit D641, dated the 14th of September, 1995. It's, again, from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan, and it's referring to the meeting with Mr. Sarinic on the 9th of September.
