And that paragraph 7 of the report that we looked at concerning discussions with Mr. Sarinic on the handling of Serb persons in the UN compound they may wish to investigate for alleged war crimes, and saying: "I agreed in principle to Sarinic's proposal but added that General Cermak and General Forand would have to agree on detail." And his direction to UNCRO is for Forand to ensure international standards are complied with prior to agreeing to detailed procedures to be proposed by Cermak. So that's where it was in UN headquarters. And D315, Exhibit D315, takes up the end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because as you will see from this document from the Chief of Staff, UNCRO, to the commander, various senior officials about the movement of the IDPs crossed -- crossing Serbia, details on what happened at Lipovac. What I'm concerned about is paragraph 2: "The initial cooperation of the Croatian military appeared to be outstanding. Colonel General Cermak, the military governor of Knin, was very friendly and helpful when we met with him on Wednesday, 14th of September, 1995, to discuss the movement plan ... he donated a truckload of clothing, arranged for food, juices for the DPs during the trip. The cooperation of the Croat police also appeared good, and they deployed a large number of police to supervise the movement of the convoy." Were you aware that the Chief of Staff of UNCRO held those views concerning Mr. Cermak's role in the matter --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- of the movement of these people?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the last document to go to is 2D05-0090.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That last document was an internal UN document and not written to Mr. Cermak. This document, dated the 20th of September, 1995, was from acting Sector South Commander Colonel Blahna. We know that General Forand was away at this date and sent to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia about the transport of refugees on the 16th and 17th of September, 1995, in accordance with UNCRO and Sector South commander's plan, and he refers to the transport there, the type of people. And in the second paragraph: "As the mentioned the humanitarian mission, various international organisations from Sector South and other agencies took part. Ones of key persons of success of this mission was Colonel Cermak, General Cermak and his liaison officers, Captain Lukovic, Lieutenant Mercer, Ensign Dondo. Thanks to their initiate and responsible actions, this mission was done successfully. Please relay my personal gratitude and thanks to General Cermak for the quick and professional arrangements." May this letter be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection. I kind of recall seeing the letter before but I still have no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I asked Colonel Leslie, I think it was about it; I asked someone, and it wasn't traced. It may have gone in as an exhibit with General Forand. I might have made a mistake, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can neither confirm nor deny whether you made a mistake, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps proper attention would be given to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have information now, it is similar to Colonel Leslie's letter. It's not the same. Colonel Leslie wrote one that I put to him -- I suggested to him and he -- he didn't have it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So apparently it is not yet in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, it's another letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good always to see that you didn't make a mistake. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If this could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D897.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D897 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, there it is, that is the story of the displaced persons, Mr. Liborius, and the people alleged to have committed war crimes from the documents at the time. Don't you agree they show a very different picture from your assessment some years later that this was a game to General Cermak, and he wanted to get out as many people from the UN camp as he could. Don't you agree you have been unfair on him?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I will be repeating myself, but I think it is worth that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, there is no need to repeat yourself. The question simply was whether, having looked at all this material you now consider your assessment a couple of years after the events unfair or not. That's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Liborius? Mr. Liborius, Mr. Kuzmanovic is Defence counsel for Mr. Markac, and he will now cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Still good morning, Mr. Liborius. Five more minutes.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, I'm going to concentrate my questions on two areas, and hopefully we'll be done in rather short order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could please call up 3D01-0053.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And while that is coming up, Mr. Liborius, you had, through the course of your work, done assessments of damages to buildings, including religious buildings in Sector South; correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I noted at least in the documentation that you put together that you did not delineate whether or not, for example, to religious buildings in Sector South there was damage to Catholic churches. Is that a correct assessment on my part?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please explain delineate whether or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. When you would put together your list of damages to religious buildings you did not make a separate category for, for example orthodox churches or Catholic church correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly correct, party correct. If we happened in our monitoring activity to be in the position to establish whether it was an orthodox church we would do so. As I said earlier, the compilation of the ECMM database was not done by me in the final version. I think that -- does that satisfy your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure you played a role there it but you played more of a reporting role; correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in that role of reporting, did you -- is it fair to say that did you not refer to any Croatian governmental information on destruction that occurred before Operation Storm began?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you rely on any information that would have been provided by the Croatian government on destruction to buildings whether they're religious or other buildings in Sector South before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would as a monitor gather as much information I could on beforehand. Should that information also happen to have Croatian government source that will only be a further ground on which you could conduct your monitoring, so I did not exclude it. I'm not sure I fully understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, the question simply is whether you relied on any government information about the destruction which stemmed from before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did take in as much information as I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did that include government information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall anyone within the Croatian government that you spoke to specifically about war damages to Sector South before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time in conversations with the Croatian army liaison officers, it would also be one of the topics we would deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as a name or a member of what ministry other than a Croatian liaison officer you cannot tell us specifically. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think some of the names that were mentioned before by Mr. Kay I did discuss that issue from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before you --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lukovic and Dondo and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before you is a letter dated September 1st signed by Dr. Ivan Simonovic, at the time the assistant minister of foreign affairs enclosing some statistical information in particular about damage and population before and after Operation Storm? Did you ever meet or speak with Dr. Simonovic at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Dr. Simonovic is?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that he is currently the minister of justice of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the second page. In the second paragraph of page 2, the paragraph begins --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite small, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The document begins: "Prior to the onset of Serb aggression in 1991, there were 581.633 ethnic Serbs (or 12.2 per cent of the population) in Croatian." Were you aware of that figure?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12 per cent or so would correspondence basically to my prior knowledge, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now the next sentence states: "Serbs made up a majority in only 11 municipalities." And then I'll skip the parenthetical: "In which they made up 144.200 of the 195.000 residents or less than one quarter of all Croatian Serbs." Were you aware at all of that population break down in those municipalities, until now?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this develops into a statistical exercise, let me also with reference to your previous question refer to what I said when we last met, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, hang on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did use the information that was provided for instance in the statistical book that the government of Croatia had issued prior. I think I called it the big blue book earlier, and whenever there was a need to see some statistics I would most often solicit information from that source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So the answer to my question was yes?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To which question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware at all of that population break down in those municipalities until now as I read them to you. I'm not asking you for an exact quote but your recollection was that the blue book contained this type of population break down. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statistical information I had at the time was that there was municipalities prior to the war in 1991 where Serbs made up the majority, there were some areas where ethnic Croatians -- ethnic Croats were in the majority, but the population figure was roughly about 15 per cent or so. That's you say here 12.2. I used sometimes as a rule of thumb around 15 per cent but I don't think that makes a dig difference here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not my number it's the number contained in what the Croatian government has provided in this particular document.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can scroll down please the sentence is the third from the bottom beginning: "As a consequence." "As a consequence and the consequence is what happened between 1991 and 1995, it is estimated that only 184.000 Serbs remained in the occupied territories in 1994. It is interesting to note that less than three per cent of the overall population in Croatia controlled over one quarter of the country." Now, Mr. Liborius, in your review of the population numbers and in preparing your report were you aware of that figure of 184.000 Serbs remaining in the occupied territories in 1994.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did recall that I considered the official population figure given by the so-called government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was -- I considered that inflated and that there were less people. Now I always treated exact figures or alleged exact figures with some caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this number of 184.000 Serbs would you agree or disagree with that number as provided by the government of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you ask me today a number I would adopt the same pattern of -- of work as I did, that I like to see some of my notes and I like to go through some of the papers. I'm not in the business of saying now several years later whether 184 or 150 or 200 is the exact number; and I don't think that is fair if I have to give an exact answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the fair to state that you can't agree and you can't disagree you don't know?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is fair to say that if I'm asked a specific question about some of these details I'll have to return to papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What papers would you need to return to?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, provided that I'm given the time by my government, I will return to the blue book, return to the documents I produced myself. I return to UNHCR figures. I'll return to ICRC figures they were quite accurate sometimes. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's assume for a minute that this 184.000 Serbs is that within the range of population that you would think would have been in that area as of 1994?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't sound out wild. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How about the three per cent of the population controlling other one quarter of the country. Is there any disagreement that you would have with that? You would agree that one quarter of Croatia was occupied by the Serbs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. The general picture that the occupied territories were quite scarcely populated as opposed to the coastal area, Zagreb and the larger Croatian towns in Slovenia. That is an a fair description of how I saw the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with me, Mr. Liborius, that most of the Serbs in Croatia the larger portion of the Serbs was located in the cities rather than in Sector South before the war broke out, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the ethnic composition as I recall it was that there were many Serbs living in the larger Croatian towns, including Zagreb, and that -- I don't know the exact number, I should say, I have to look that up, and that the Krajina areas from having a majority Serb population at the onset of the war and very brutally Krajina Serb military and police and all the people expelled ethnic Croats and that reduced the number of population inside the -- inside the -- the Krajina areas, that some of the Serbs that had lived in cities in Croatia like Zagreb and Split and other areas, that they -- during the war years, so to speak, filtered out, left the area. They may have still had legal registration there, but from time to time you would come across stories and information and evidence suggesting that they felt it more secure to leave that, going via either Hungary to Serbia so that I'm just walking you through some of these statistical issues you would have to take into consideration when you dealt with population figures, because they were always used for a political purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to use them for political purpose here. I'm just using this particular document and asking you that if we look at the 184.000 Serbs that are listed in this document as remaining in the occupied territories and you compare them with the 580.000 or so ethnic Serbs of the population of Croatia you would you agree with me that the majority of Serbs lived in Croatia lived not in the areas that were occupied but in areas outside the occupied parts of Croatia. If you look at purely the numbers.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the numbers for Sector East and I think that also contained a couple of -- of towns with a considerable population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But generally you would you agree with me, would you not? Using the numbers that -- assuming that the numbers here in that aide-memoire are correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mean that the majority of the Serbs that lived in Croatia during the time lived not in Sector South or Sector North, in what were termed the occupied territories or in Sector East and West for that matter but in unoccupied parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time there was a bit of inflate of statistics when it came to Serbs living or having at least registered as residents in the Croatian towns but in fact not living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So you can't agree with me or you can agree?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a matter of agreeing or disagreeing. I think the general accepted fact was that the Krajina area had during the war years become an area where only very, very small pockets of ethnic Croats lived under the observation of among others ECMM. I visited some of the hamlets, and UNPROFOR forces; but it was an area where previously there had been more people and that also part of the Serbs, the Krajina Serbs, who lived there before the war as a consequence of the general insecurity they themselves also left. I know many who left for Banja Luka for Serbia proper, so that it was a -- quite an ethnically pure area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. I do understand that, Mr. Liborius. I guess my question and I will ask it one more time and then we will move on. Using the figures in the aide-memoire if have you have 581.000 or so ethnic Serbs that live in Croatia, and 184.000 of them live or remained in the occupied territories would you agree with me using these numbers that the majority, the vast majority of ethnic Serbs lived outside of the occupied areas.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you use the figures here 597 -- what is it 597, is certainly more than 184.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll move on. Thank you, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we go to the next page of this document, please, at the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The destruction of churches is discussed in the -- beginning at the end of the second line. It says: "For example, of the 164 Catholic churches in the recently liberated territories, 154 or 94 per cent had been damaged or destroyed. In comparison of the 114 Serbian orthodox churches, 97 or 85 per cent are undamaged and are presently being looked after by Croatian civil authorities. Added to this is the complete destruction of many Croatian towns and villages, amounting to direct material damages of over 23 billion USD." Now, Mr. Liborius, I want to ask you specifically because you did at least in terms your reporting an analysis of the damages done to buildings, particularly in some cases churches were you aware of the statistical differences in, for example, religious destruction when you compiled your report?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should perhaps underline that the area I worked in did have more Serb majority areas as opposed to other areas of the occupied territories, in particular Sector West, of course, and that of course the damage to Catholic churches, for example the -- the church in Knin, was also a factor. It was clear to us at that time in 1995 that as the Serb forces would have had control over the Krajina area for many years they would certainly not have destroyed Serbian orthodox churches. I did not recall that many Catholic churches; but I of course know of, as I said some of them being destroyed. And of course Serbia orthodox churches would be by the Krajina leaders considered their own churches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 5 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Contained in this document, Mr. Liborius, are -- starting on page 5, six pages worth of description of destruction of particular Catholic churches and it does combine Sectors North and South; for example, you are familiar with the area of Drnis, correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And obviously there are tens of churches or religious buildings here that were damaged or destroyed. Can you tell me, when you conducted your analysis of damage were you including any of these buildings for example that you observed in Drnis?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I think we have to distinguish between two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assessments that we were instructed to start compiling on a more systematic fashion shortly after Operation Storm had ended focussed mainly on residential accommodations, houses an apartments, and so on. Of course, from time to time we would also include references to religious sites, and for example, in the areas where if a large burnings of a hamlet was going on and one particular church was being guarded and spared, we would of course notice that. You ask about Drnis and whether I'm familiar with that, of course I think my recollection was that in particular in the pink zones where the fighting had been going on also, the -- the destruction of churches of course did take place, most deplorable I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And under Knin, Knin was not in a pink zone. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And there are eight religious buildings there that were --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- destroyed. The city of Benkovac too was not a pink zone was it?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And Obrovac was not in a pink zone?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'll skip over the next few pages because they involve Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But if we go to page 11, please. If we could go all the way so we see the top, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This lists the state of orthodox churches and monasteries in the liberated areas of former Sectors North and South and obviously the first three areas are in Sector North, correct? Drnis or Sector South?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you see at least what is documented here is that the vast majority of these almost all of these buildings are undamaged and secured by police patrols. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only see the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I at frequent occasions mentioned also in my reports that the orthodox churches monasteries and so on were being guarded by military personnel. I talked with the guards from time to time and that spared them destruction at least for sometime. I did come back later once the guards had been removed and then some of them had been burned down but that's another story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't have listed that in any report, do you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That the churches were burned down some later time when you came back?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of my tenure in Sector South, I think, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is it September 1st, this report is dated September 1st. If you look at the second page here, for example, under Knin there are 17 buildings of religious Serbian religious -- 17 Serbian religious buildings all of which are undamaged other than the last one where there is it damage, and it is being secured?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I talked with the guy at the Krka monastery one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the same thing with Benkovac and Gracac on the following page. And again Obrovac which is also Sector South. Right?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay, I'm sorry to inform you that you did make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You tendered the letter in which received number D897 but it is D316 already. So therefore, D897 is now -- can now be used for the last document tendered by Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D897 is now again admitted into evidence. But it's a different number. It's 3D -- if you could help me out --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour, 3D01-0053.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That document is now admitted under D897. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, I'm going to move to a different topic now and this is my last topic which has some more documents involved with it. During the course of the summary of your testimony that was written out -- read during your direct examination, and I'll read a portion of and ask you some questions about it. Part of the summary of the 92 ter submission states --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, necessary to remind you that the summary is just to inform the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if there's any -- if it speeds up matters then it's fine but it would lead to discussion whether the summary reflects what ask in the statement then of course we lose time. I'll leave it to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll be very brief and it's not going to be a big read, it is only two sentences, three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I am going to ask you some questions about it so keep it in mind,

utterances.speaker: MR. LIBORIUS
utterances.text: "It's described that during Operation Storm he witnessed the shelling of Knin and observed the firing of multiple rocket systems. Witness 127," which is you, "Personally observed crime incidents within Sector South during the weeks following the shelling. They included looting, burning of houses, farms and property as well as destruction of livestock by HV troops and special police." Now the last two words special police that's what I want to focus on with you, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we go to P815, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, this is your report dated August 26th of 1995 which you wrote entitled the consequences in former RSK of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initial consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. While the report says the subject: The consequences and in the report it is titled the initial consequences?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We're both correct on that one. On the very last page of this document, unfortunately, my document itself isn't numbered except for the stamps. It's 5933 is the last page. Annex B. Now I will submit to that you in your -- in this entire document, Mr. Liborius, including your overview where you describe living conditions, factors behind destruction, conclusions, and including the Annex A, which are certain day-to-day observations there is no one mention of special police in your report. Do you have any reason to disagree with me? I guess if you need -- go ahead, sorry.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I interpret your question here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go -- I'll go to the last page on Annex B. Where you state: "This annex is an account of the personnel and the groups observed by ECMM either doing looting or burning, the ECMM teams are operating in the southern part of Sector South." And you highlight in capital letters, "THE UNITS INVOLVED" and then you list the ECMM have witnessed the following type of people of groups involved in burning and looting, and this list does not include anywhere in it special police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list here with numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4, the purpose of that was to describe faces in the appearance and what went on. It does not distinguish HV Home Guard units. The distinction that was underlying these faces here was -- was that military police, was it military police and civilians, was it mainly civilians. So the purpose of this here was not to say in this particular it was Home Guard, it was Guards Brigade, this was special police, this was ordinary police, that was not the purpose here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did I ask you, sir, what the purpose was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, your question was unclear. Your question was unclear whether this includes -- we should make a distinction between whether the report mentions specifically or whether it could include in any of the categories mentioned. That question is unspecific; and therefore, I think your last response was not the best. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Special police is not included anywhere in Annex B. Is that correct, Mr. Liborius? You say: Croatian civil police you say HV military personnel, but do you not include special police on annex B. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is it correct that special police is not mentioned on the paper in front of us. It is my recollection that the special police issue that is reflected in the -- in the resume became more relevant after this annex was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're going to get into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go to P799, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: P799, sir, is your statement of November 2nd, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we go to the -- the Bates number is on the bottom, it's 9360.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You specifically discuss at the very top of this document check-points manned by HV MP. That's Croatian military and military police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Or Croatian army military police and CRO policija that's the Croatian police, correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was meant when I say Croatian policija, I distinguished -- I did distinction between army and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, nowhere --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having various elements of the police covered in that expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nowhere here is special police mentioned, correct, of the word special police or the description of a unit called special police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now you know -- do you know what the special police was?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, special police, and it was told to me it was used sometimes to do mopping up operations. It was used to conduct operations in certain specified areas. We would, from time to time, be informed that the unit operated in a certain area we could not access was because it was special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Activity?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Activity, what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Because there was special police activities going on?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see the special police?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time we would come across them. I think the -- the interim garrisons that they used, mainly they were looking a bit like -- like army facilities, high in number. They would all of course have the police cars with the police insignia, that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of cars did they have?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have four-wheel drives. They would have various other vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And where did you see them? You said from time to time you would see them. Where?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall we saw an area around Gracac. I think coming out of Donji Lapac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What did the soldiers look like, the special police soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did they have?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them I saw would have -- I say more combat-type police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Which is what? What colour?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them would be as blueish thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Blueish?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of those I saw, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Silver?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Silver what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Uniforms. Grey or silver uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grey, what do you call it? I'm not good at colours in English. Dusk grey-blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sort of a blueish colour?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The kind of -- the.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be kind of like the colour of this grey?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes sprinkled with a bit more blue but sometimes. Sometimes also just blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, for the record would you describe the colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure I was use the grey of the mouse pad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a grey mouse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some would have fatigue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether it was on the video. Of course, for later instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: To have a laugh about it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not trying to make jokes. In order to enable them to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll look for the video camera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just see whether this could be on the video. I do not dare to describe it. The problem is that this is an instruction if the Presiding Judge speaks he should be on the screen, so I'll keep my mouth shut for a second so that the cameras can cover the colour of your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I will model the colour of the uniform as described by Mr. Liborius by pointing with my pen here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P8303, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic I'm also looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have about three more of the statements to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would it take approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we first need to have a break for various reasons. Mr. Kay you're on your foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, for personal reasons I can't be here, and I have to leave straight away, now. Ms. Higgins and Mr. Cayley will be in charge of matters in my absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. We will have a break first and we will resume at 1.00, and I'm confident that we will be able to release Mr. Liborius by quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I had a quick discussion with Mr. Waespi and P803 which is the statement of September 2008 of the supplementary witness statement. He's agreed there is no mention of the special police in this particular statement so will not go through it. Am I right, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you told me, that there is no mention of the special police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you agreed Mr. Waespi. That's what Mr. Kuzmanovic presented. And you have now -- you know what's said at weddings open your mouth now or never do it again, just on this matter, of course. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could go to P801, please. And page 3 of P801.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And while it's coming up, Mr. Liborius, this is your statement of October 2005. And at the top of this page, you mention that there was special police headquarters in Gracac and that you had two meetings with the special police in Donji Lapac. I will take those two separately. First the special police headquarters in Gracac, that was something that you observed?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you say you had two meetings with the special police in Donji Lapac. You recall who you met with?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have to look into the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to D?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The meeting -- was at least two meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to D743, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's your notebook, Mr. Liborius. And if we could go the last four numbers of the page are 3541. Mr. Liborius, I don't know if you're are similarly marked but the Bates numbers of your original is on the upper right-hand corner. There is a Bate stamp number 06353541. If not, can I give you the date. It's 29 September of 1995. Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And here it's -- you note: "Police vehicle," something "D. Lapac." Can you read that what is the word in between VEH for vehicle and D. Lapac. Can you read that in your original?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not so clear in my own original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll move further down. Two lines below that you have CRO special police is sighted in Dubrovnik. That is not anywhere near Donji Lapac is it?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is under the heading, UNMO sit brief, 29 September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then below have you CP, and I assume that is COP or CP?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entry COP, Donji Lapac, that is chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you met with the chief of police in Donji Lapac. There is it no mention of special police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one here, Donji Lapac was an area that we visited from time to time. So if your question suggests what was going on on the 29th September; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- your statement said that you had at least two meetings with the special police in Donji Lapac and what I'm submit to go you is I have gone through your notes which is the particular exhibit, 743 and I -- other than the designation of special police being cited in Dubrovnik on this 29 of September 1995 entry you note: "Chief of police Donji Lapac," that to me is the chief of the regular police, is it not? You met with them frequently in your visit?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah if we could go to the team report on that particular date, we can solve the uncertainties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do that in a minute. But at least as far as your handwritten notes are concerned there is no notation that you met on this date with the special police in Donji Lapac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on that particular date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go to 3543 of your notes, which is, I think, Mr. Liborius, two pages on in your original. If we could go to the top. Again you've got COP, chief of police on the upper left, Donji Lapac, correct.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Piplica was the person who was the chief of police there Donji Lapac, was he not?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I would assume that from my notes but if we go to the team report then we can sort out the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Below that there's another entry of Piplica with an arrow pointing down if we could scroll down right there; "COP," something "contact," correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Establishes contact, escape of contact, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, in this particular document, again there is no mention of a meeting with the special police in Donji Lapac in this note. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on this page, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then if we could go to 3558. The very top of the document. If we could move the document -- there we go, 6 of October 1995. Again, handwritten: Meet with Mr. Piplica, D. Lapac.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When you get to the original, Mr. Liborius, let me know.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the very top, meeting with Mr. Piplica, D. Lapac do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Another mention of Donji Lapac but no mention in your notes of meeting with the special police, correct? At least not on this page?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, 3559. And the bottom third of the page. Again, chief of police, D. Lapac. No mention of the special police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be mistaken your meetings with the chiefs of police, Mr. Liborius? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Donji Lapac was a place we visited from time to time, and it was a -- the short answer to your question is I don't think; and I will explain you why. Donji Lapac was a place we visited from time to time. It was in our patrol area. Donji Lapac was, as you will recall the geography, the area that was to the north of Knin, and it was important to the -- to the access to the -- to the mountains regions, to Bosnia; and it was an area where, of course as the mountains region suggested, it was a hilly area and therefore from time to time it was used as, if you wish, an area where you would hold larger number of -- of police, special police also from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless, at least not in your handwritten diary of the areas that we've covered for Donji Lapac -- strike that question. I will rephrase it. This handwritten diary you made contemporaneous with your day, correct, normally?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My handwritten diary here as you can see it is the notes taken to the particular meeting. Now, I did not always do the note-taking. Some of my monitoring colleagues would do that from time to time. We would split that between us. So to suggest that the fact that there's no mention of a special police suggests that there is it no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, Mr. Liborius. If you would stop asking yourself what is suggested or what is in the mind of the one who puts the question and if you just answer the question, that is whether the handwritten diary you made contemporaneous with your day, whether that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Contemporaneous ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you write it down at the time you experienced these meetings, events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to 3579, at the very top, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's the 13th of October, 1995, Mr. Liborius, for your original. Again, at the top it's noted in your diary 13 October 1995, Donji Lapac, new COP, meaning chief of police, Donji Lapac, plus outgoing COP, chief of police. Again, at least as of this date, 13 October 1995, there is no specific mention of meeting with the special police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will submit to you, Mr. Liborius, that through your entire diary other than the one entry where you mentioned on page 3541 that the Croatian special police is sighted in Dubrovnik. There is no mention of meetings with special police in your handwritten diary, D743. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It touches on the question, what is in this diary? Is this [Realtime transcript read in error "this is"] the only true reflection of my monitoring activity? It is not. So in order to -- part of one question is yes. Part two is, this is not everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to D741. D741 --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just correct the transcript in my answer? I said, "is this the only true reflection," not "this is." It's a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Transcript, Mr. Liborius, is worked on after we have left this courtroom and then with great precision as we are aware of transcribers and those assisting outside this courtroom take care that we have the best transcript that could be possibly with us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The D741, Mr. Liborius, is you calendar which is another document in which you put handwritten notes on. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't make notes in my calendar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And if we go to the entry for Tuesday, 29 August, you're discussing Plavno-Gracac. And if we move to the -- in the type written version, fifth line. It's actually 29, there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You're speaking about the town of Gracac and you mention: "Special police are using the city as a support point." And you put in quotation marks "special police." You observed that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier in that same entry you put COP, chief of police. That's something that you use very frequently that abbreviation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that COP chief of police, that is of the local police station? Correct.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most instances, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now if we go to your diary or your same exhibit calendar entry: Friday, 1 September. At the very top you note: "Meeting, Donji Lapac, close to Bihac, with chief of police?" Now again the meeting you have in Donji Lapac does not mention that you had a meeting with the special police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And if we go to your entry on Friday, 6 October. And while we're waiting for the English to come up, here we go: "Forward control basis we patrol in Donji Lapac municipality." There's no mention in there of meeting with anyone object that particular day. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's patrol base, for what patrol base in the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So the translation is not correct. It should say, Forward patrol base, we patrol in Donji Lapac municipality.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a patrol we would usual stop and try to have a talk about the people we would encounter, especially during at Donji Lapac patrol where there was very little number of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So at least --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So if we would try to portray what happened on 6th of October, shouldn't we go to the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We could do that. I'm using this, Mr. Liborius, your underlying personal documents, your diary and your calendar, to try to discover evidence of whether or not you met with the special police. And at least as of Friday, 6 October, there is no mention of chief of police or special police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no mention on page -- Friday, 6 October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Kuzmanovic it is it asked again and again if the word "special police" appears. Of course, that could be done in a bit more efficient way. I mean, of course, the Chamber can read the words "special police" would not remain unnoticed if we see so ... Please proceed. And, of course, I take that you give an opportunity to the witness to -- to correct when our reading is wrong or to explain. At the same time it ends up always in the same is ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, if we could go to P801, page 5 at the very bottom. Second -- the single sentence that is above the last paragraph. This statement you gave, Mr. Liborius, in October 2005, which is ten years after Operation Storm, this sentence is the one and only sentence in all of your statements where you say something about the special police and crimes. You say: "I also witnessed special police vehicles in the vicinity where crimes had just been committed." Now, I'd like to ask you, you don't describe what kind of crimes have just been committed where special police vehicles were in the vicinity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. In that particular sentence, no that is not described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What places or villages or towns were there in which you witnessed special police vehicles in the vicinity where crimes had just been committed.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in the area of Donji Lapac and the long stretch up to that particular area, you travel through, travel through a village called Srb and Donji Srb; and you travel through areas where there was very, very little civil activity, so to speak. And I remember one particular instances where we were blocked from entering I think it was Srb or Donji Srb on the way north and once we had or one of my team members had made a call back to headquarters in Knin and we had lifted this restriction of movement we entered through the area and we saw a lot of destruction recently been done, and the only vehicles we encountered in that, so to speak, restricted box was special police vehicles. That suggested to me that there was no other people that we had been blocked access, we were perhaps unexpected guests at that particular time, and that once we gained access insisting on our freedom of movement that had been promised to us earlier that we came across an area where the only vehicles that was special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand you say you saw vehicles, but what crimes had just been committed?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arson and destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you attributed that to the special police?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you actually see the special police allegedly committing these crimes?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I write: "In the vicinity where crimes had just been committed." We all perfectly well know why at certain times, these boxes of restriction of movement was imposed and once you get in there and you see special police in the vicinity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I write.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question simply was whether you observed it, personally. I think the circumstances are clear and apparently what you conclude out of that is maybe clear as well. Of course it is for the Chamber to draw conclusions, and it is for you to answer the question. You did not personally observe the commission of these crimes? And you described the circumstances under which you wrote down that they recently had been committed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you not gives us a date here anywhere in this statement ten years after the events. Can you give me a date?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A specific date would require me to go through a lot of documentations. But I remember the Donji Srb and the Srb incident. But a specific date I have to peruse through the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How many days after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Long after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the vehicles for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say long after.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Weeks after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four-wheel drive vehicles, police insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What colour?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue and white and different insignias, different types of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any people next to the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- in the Srb and Donji Srb indent we saw people walking around in the forest and field areas. I did not see them close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were these the same people with the silvery-blue uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some had this blueish fatigue as well. I think the fatigue was omitted once we had the overlapping speakers, but that is not the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just about done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, had you ever spoken to anybody about your witnessing the special police vehicles in the vicinity where crimes had been just committed, like the local police, like any military personnel?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I brought up at a number of meetings with the Croatian officials that they should actually do more to control the episodes that were going on in the area. It was a frequent topic, if not in every meeting then in every second meeting or so. The level of lack of proper activity was obvious, and I think the Croatian authorities once we mentioned it again and again and again got tired because they would ask the question. We knew what they would say; there were rogue elements. But I mentioned it frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking about the specific incident when you were in Srb or Donji Srb wherever the place was regarding you impression that his was the special police. Did you report this to anyone?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I got to Donji Lapac at a later meeting having just gone through one of these areas that had been -- were burning was takes place, I made that a point in one of the meetings saying, You have been telling me that you will control the episodes for weeks and why do I still encounter them when I go through the country?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, last question. Would you agree with me --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And no answer was given by the way for completion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that when you refer to the special police that you may be confusing the special police with the regular police?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If people tell me that you cannot enter this certain area because this is an special police operating going on; and we go through an area, and we clearly see that it is not HV/Croatian army units and it is police units, not just a check-point or traffic police, then I would say -- I tend to believe when people tell me, Oh there is an special police unit there, there that is a special police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You can't tell me who told you. It is just your impression?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also we had the Srb and Donji Srb episode. I was informed -- I think my teammate made the telephone call to the Knin headquarters there and the reply was there was a special police operation going on, and that was told to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm through. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Liborius to very short follow-up questions. You said once I got to Donji Lapac at a later meeting, having just gone through one of these area, a meeting with whom in Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the meeting with not both of chief of police and the local governor, then the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you specifically, when you, so to say, reported this or mentioned this, did you specifically say that the special police was involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said we had just passed through an area where we were told that a special police operation was going on and we saw police vehicles on the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, one very brief topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, when you testified last time in your cross-examination with Mr. Misetic, you were asked about a meeting with General Gotovina on the 27th of October, and your daily report from the 28th of October, and there is P822.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if it could be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember being cross-examined and indeed examined about that meeting with General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just have a look again at the document, and in particular at the second page of the English version. Do you recall the topic and you drafting this document as a report of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now let me ask you, first of all did you report -- did your report from that date, 28th of October, include every single -- single thing that happened during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think we have been through that in quite detail. And as I said at that time it was a meeting where the HRC Gambotti also had a say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We don't neat to rehash it. If can you just focus on whether you reported every single thing or not.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your answer is did you report every single word that was spoken?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: My next question is that you told Mr. Misetic at pages 8428 to 8430 that you wrote in the daily report of 28th October 1995 was not the whole truth. Now my question to you is: Did you ever write anything in your report that you knew was false?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So when you said that it may not have been the whole truth, what did you mean by that, if you can be as brief as you can.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief. It was, as I said, a report that also reflected the way Colonel Gambotti wanted the meeting to be reported, and my notes from the meeting illustrates that there was a -- an acceptance on the side of General Gotovina of the issue put to him by Colonel Gambotti that it was in fact a lack of control. There was extraordinary events as he called it that was going on, and he failed to control that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, as you rightly observed, we have covered that. Just your notion that the report didn't contain the whole truth. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explanation is there was a certain rapport between Mr. Gambotti and the General, and perhaps Mr. Gambotti felt that he had obtained sufficient information for his future function as HRC but that in this particular daily report, which he asked me to sign off on, that he would, so to speak suppress that particular element.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will have less than five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than five minutes. Could I ask other counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just have a moment, my case manager just needs to switch places with the Markac case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. It's now on the record that I made the same mistake twice yesterday by not finishing our session in open session. And now again this morning by not moving from private session to open session when we are at the point of adjourning. I thanked in private session Mr. Liborius so that is on record for the public as well that I thank you in the usual way. I would like to add to this, that I want to apologise to interpreters, transcribers for not having sought their consent in taking 15 more minutes than was announced. We will therefore, also, start this afternoon 15 minutes later. That is, that is we will start at 3.00 so as to give everyone at least some time for lunch. We'll then hear the witness who testified in closed session. Could the parties give me an indication as whether there would be a fair chance also looking at the schedule that was distributed whether there's a chance that we could finish that witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I passed through my notes and I believe I wouldn't take more than an hour and a half, maybe even less, an hour. I will try to do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe we can finish him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Also for planning and scheduling purposes, let's assume that we will finish that witness today. Mr. Liborius, again, a good journey home. We will resume at 3.00 this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 2.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, we'll move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. So even with the curtains down I announce that we'll adjourn for the day and that we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 7th of November, at quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom I. And if there would be anyone in the public gallery at this time, he has to live with this shortage of his rights to observe this court proceedings. We stand adjourned but not until after I have thanked interpreters and all those assisting us, including security, for having again stolen seven minutes of your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
